items.stem: A laboratory without a spectrophotometer considers the alkali hematin method for hemoglobin. Why is this method unsuitable for specimens from newborns?
options: Hb F resists denaturation by alkali, so it is not fully converted
Newborn red cells are too large to lyse in sodium hydroxide
High newborn bilirubin bleaches the alkali hematin color
Hb F binds cyanide instead of forming alkali hematin
items.why: In the alkali hematin method, sodium hydroxide converts hemoglobin to alkaline hematin, whose color is compared with a standard. **Fetal hemoglobin resists alkali denaturation, so in newborn blood with much Hb F the conversion is incomplete and the result is falsely low.** The same property of Hb F is the basis of the alkali denaturation test for Hb F.

whyNot.1: Newborn macrocytes lyse readily in hypotonic or alkaline reagents; cell size is not the problem.
whyNot.2: Bilirubin is a source of interference in some photometric methods, but it does not explain the specific failure with Hb F.
whyNot.3: No cyanide is used in the alkali hematin method; cyanide is a reagent in the cyanmethemoglobin method.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemoglobin determination section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hemoglobinopathies chapter

items.stem: In the cyanmethemoglobin method, which component of Drabkin reagent oxidizes the ferrous (Fe2+) heme iron of hemoglobin to the ferric (Fe3+) state?
items.why: Drabkin reagent works in two steps. **Potassium ferricyanide oxidizes hemoglobin iron to the ferric state, forming methemoglobin (hemiglobin).** Potassium cyanide then combines with methemoglobin to form stable cyanmethemoglobin, which is read at 540 nm.

whyNot.0: Cyanide acts in the second step, binding methemoglobin to form cyanmethemoglobin; it does not oxidize the iron.
whyNot.2: The detergent lyses red cells and reduces turbidity; it has no oxidizing role.
whyNot.3: The phosphate buffer shortens the conversion time so the tube can be read sooner; it does not oxidize iron.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemoglobin determination section; CLSI H15

items.stem: A patient with sickle cell anemia has a spun microhematocrit of 28%, while the analyzer's calculated hematocrit (RBC x MCV) is 25%. The centrifuge was recently calibrated and the tube was spun for the validated time. What best explains the difference?
options: Excess EDTA shrank the red cells before the microhematocrit was spun
Sickled cells hemolyzed in the capillary tube during centrifugation
Sickled cells pack poorly and trap extra plasma in the red cell column
The buffy coat was left out of the packed-cell reading
items.why: Rigid or abnormally shaped red cells do not pack tightly, so more plasma stays trapped among them. **Increased trapped plasma makes the spun hematocrit read higher than the calculated hematocrit.** The same effect occurs with spherocytes, macrocytes and hypochromic cells, while the calculated hematocrit is unaffected by packing.

whyNot.0: Excess EDTA shrinks red cells and would lower, not raise, the spun hematocrit.
whyNot.1: Hemolysis in the tube would shrink the packed-cell column and lower the spun hematocrit, not raise it.
whyNot.3: Leaving the buffy coat out of the reading is correct technique; including it would be the error that raises the value.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hematocrit section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hematology procedures chapter

items.stem: During a Westergren ESR, the rack holding one tube is found to be leaning a few degrees from vertical for the full hour. How does this affect that patient's result?
options: The ESR is unaffected if the reading is taken at exactly 60 minutes
The ESR is unaffected because rouleaux formation is unchanged
items.why: Red cells in a tilted tube slide down the lower wall while plasma rises along the upper wall, which speeds settling. **Even a tilt of a few degrees can raise the ESR markedly, so tubes must be kept exactly vertical.** Other technical errors that raise the ESR include high room temperature and vibration.

whyNot.0: Tilting speeds sedimentation; it does not slow it.
whyNot.1: Correct timing does not cancel the error; the cells have already fallen faster during the hour.
whyNot.2: Even with normal rouleaux, the tilt itself speeds the fall of the red cell column.

items.ref: ICSH review of the measurement of the ESR (2011); CLSI H02; Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., ESR section

items.stem: A patient with an acute inflammatory illness has a high plasma fibrinogen and a markedly raised ESR. How does fibrinogen speed up sedimentation?
options: It lowers the zeta potential, so red cells stack into rouleaux
It increases plasma viscosity, so single red cells fall faster
It lyses red cells, so the red cell column drops more quickly
It makes red cells spherical, so they sink with less drag
items.why: Red cells normally carry a negative surface charge (mainly from sialic acid) that makes them repel each other. **Large, asymmetric plasma proteins such as fibrinogen reduce this repulsive zeta potential, so the cells stack into rouleaux that sediment much faster than single cells.** Albumin has the opposite effect and slows the ESR.

whyNot.1: Higher viscosity would slow the fall of red cells; the faster ESR is due to aggregation, not viscosity.
whyNot.2: Fibrinogen does not lyse red cells; lysis would not create a clear plasma-cell boundary in any case.
whyNot.3: Spherocytes do not form rouleaux well and actually lower the ESR; fibrinogen does not change red cell shape.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., ESR section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hematology procedures chapter

items.stem: A laboratory runs the modified Westergren ESR on EDTA blood. According to ICSH and CLSI, how should the EDTA blood be prepared before it is drawn into the tube?
options: Dilute 1 part blood with 4 parts saline or 3.8% citrate
Dilute 4 parts blood with 1 part saline or 3.8% citrate
Use the EDTA blood undiluted, without any added diluent
Dilute 9 parts blood with 1 part distilled water
items.why: The modified Westergren method allows ESR testing from the same EDTA tube used for the CBC. **EDTA blood is diluted 4:1 with saline or citrate (for example 2 mL blood plus 0.5 mL diluent), matching the dilution of the original citrate method.** The diluted blood is then drawn into a 200-mm Westergren tube and read at 60 minutes.

whyNot.0: This reverses the ratio and would dilute the red cells fivefold, giving a falsely rapid ESR.
whyNot.2: Undiluted EDTA blood is used in the Wintrobe method; the Westergren method requires the 4:1 dilution.
whyNot.3: Distilled water would lyse the red cells, and 9:1 is the citrate ratio for coagulation tubes.

items.ref: ICSH review of the measurement of the ESR (2011); CLSI H02; Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., ESR section

items.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has a normocytic anemia. A Prussian blue stain of the bone marrow aspirate is reviewed. Which finding is expected?
options: Absent iron in macrophages with no sideroblasts
Ringed sideroblasts making up 15% of erythroid precursors
Normal macrophage iron with many sideroblasts
Increased iron in macrophages with few sideroblasts
items.why: In anemia of chronic inflammation, hepcidin traps iron inside macrophages and blocks its release to developing red cells. **The marrow therefore shows plentiful or increased storage iron in macrophages but few iron-containing erythroid precursors (sideroblasts).** This pattern separates it from iron deficiency, in which storage iron is absent.

whyNot.0: Absent macrophage iron is the marrow picture of iron deficiency anemia.
whyNot.1: Ringed sideroblasts with iron in mitochondria around the nucleus define sideroblastic anemia, not anemia of inflammation.
whyNot.2: Many sideroblasts mean iron is reaching the erythroid cells, which is not the case when hepcidin is high.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., iron metabolism and hypochromic anemias chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., anemias of disordered iron metabolism chapter

items.stem: Cytochemistry is done on a new acute leukemia. Which result most clearly classifies the blasts as myeloid rather than lymphoid?
options: Myeloperoxidase positivity in at least 3% of the blasts
Periodic acid-Schiff positivity in coarse blocks
Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase positivity in most blasts
Diffuse acid phosphatase positivity inhibited by tartrate
items.why: Myeloperoxidase is found in the primary granules of granulocytic cells and is absent from lymphoblasts. **Positivity in 3% or more of blasts is the accepted cutoff for assigning myeloid lineage.** Sudan black B gives a similar pattern, and Auer rods stain strongly with both.

whyNot.1: Coarse block PAS positivity is the pattern typical of lymphoblasts, not myeloblasts.
whyNot.2: TdT is a marker of immature lymphoid cells and is typically present in ALL.
whyNot.3: Tartrate-sensitive acid phosphatase occurs in many cell types and is not specific for myeloid lineage; T lymphoblasts often show it in a focal pattern.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., cytochemistry and acute leukemias chapters; WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours

items.stem: Marrow cells from a new acute leukemia are stained with a combined esterase stain. One population of blasts stains with naphthol AS-D chloroacetate esterase, and a second population stains with alpha-naphthyl acetate esterase that is inhibited by sodium fluoride. Which AML subtype fits best?
items.why: Naphthol AS-D chloroacetate (specific) esterase marks the neutrophilic (granulocytic) line, while fluoride-sensitive nonspecific esterase marks the monocytic line. **Two separate blast populations, one with each enzyme, indicate both lineages, which is the pattern of acute myelomonocytic leukemia.** Each population should be at least 20% of the marrow cells.

whyNot.0: In acute promyelocytic leukemia the abnormal promyelocytes stain strongly with chloroacetate esterase, but there is no separate fluoride-sensitive monocytic population.
whyNot.2: Acute monoblastic leukemia is almost purely nonspecific esterase positive, with little or no chloroacetate esterase activity.
whyNot.3: Megakaryoblasts lack the granulocytic chloroacetate esterase population and are identified by platelet glycoproteins such as CD41 and CD61, not by this two-population esterase pattern.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., cytochemistry and acute myeloid leukemia chapters; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., acute myeloid leukemias chapter

items.stem: A marrow from an adult with pancytopenia shows a large majority of immature, dysplastic erythroid precursors. Which cytochemical result would support acute erythroid leukemia?
options: Strong myeloperoxidase positivity in the erythroblasts
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase in the erythroblasts
Strong PAS positivity in the erythroblasts
A high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score
items.why: Normal erythroid precursors are PAS negative. **In acute erythroid leukemia the neoplastic erythroblasts often show strong PAS positivity, diffuse or in coarse granules.** Erythroid cells do not contain myeloperoxidase, so MPO is not used to identify them.

whyNot.0: Myeloperoxidase is found in granulocytic and monocytic cells, not in erythroid precursors.
whyNot.1: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase is a marker for hairy cell leukemia, not for erythroid neoplasms.
whyNot.3: The LAP score measures enzyme activity in mature neutrophils and does not assess erythroblasts.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., cytochemistry section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., acute myeloid leukemias chapter

items.stem: A physician orders a leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score. Which specimen is acceptable?
options: EDTA blood held overnight at 4 degrees C, then smeared
Citrated blood from a coagulation tube, smeared after 24 hours
EDTA blood smeared and air-dried for 3 days before fixing
Fresh capillary blood or heparinized blood, smeared and fixed promptly
items.why: Alkaline phosphatase activity in neutrophils declines quickly after collection and needs divalent cations such as zinc and magnesium. **EDTA chelates these cations and inhibits the enzyme, so fresh capillary blood or heparinized blood smeared and fixed within a few hours is used.** Delayed or improperly handled specimens give falsely low scores.

whyNot.0: EDTA inhibits alkaline phosphatase, and overnight storage further reduces enzyme activity.
whyNot.1: A 24-hour delay allows enzyme activity to fall, giving a falsely low score.
whyNot.2: EDTA inhibits the enzyme, and smears left unfixed for days lose activity.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., cytochemistry section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hematology procedures chapter

items.stem: A patient with beta-thalassemia minor has an osmotic fragility test. Many target cells are seen on the smear. Compared with normal red cells, what result is expected?
options: Decreased fragility: hemolysis begins at a lower NaCl concentration
Increased fragility: hemolysis begins at a higher NaCl concentration
Normal fragility, but only after 24-hour incubation at 37 degrees C
Increased fragility in the unincubated test only
items.why: Thin, flat cells such as target cells have a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and can swell a great deal before they burst. **Their osmotic fragility is decreased, so the curve shifts to the left (hemolysis starts at lower saline concentrations).** Decreased fragility is also seen in iron deficiency, sickle cell anemia and liver disease.

whyNot.1: Increased fragility is the pattern of spherocytes, which have a low surface-area-to-volume ratio.
whyNot.2: Incubation accentuates abnormal fragility, especially in hereditary spherocytosis; it does not make target cells normal.
whyNot.3: Target cells are resistant to osmotic lysis in both unincubated and incubated tests.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemolytic anemia testing section; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., red cell membrane disorders chapter

items.stem: A tube-based hemoglobin S solubility test (sodium dithionite in high-molarity phosphate buffer) is turbid, but hemoglobin electrophoresis shows no Hb S. Which specimen condition most likely caused the false-positive screen?
items.why: The solubility test depends on reduced Hb S precipitating and making the solution turbid. **Anything that makes the solution turbid, such as heavy lipemia, high plasma proteins or a very high hematocrit, can give a false-positive result.** Positive screens are confirmed by electrophoresis or HPLC.

whyNot.0: Severe anemia lowers the amount of hemoglobin in the tube and causes false-negative, not false-positive, results.
whyNot.2: Infants have mostly Hb F and little Hb S, which tends to give false-negative results.
whyNot.3: EDTA is an acceptable anticoagulant for this test and does not cause turbidity.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemoglobinopathies chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hemoglobinopathies chapter

items.stem: A hemoglobin electrophoresis is run on cellulose acetate in an alkaline buffer (pH 8.4-8.6). Of the following, which hemoglobin ends up farthest from the point of application, toward the anode?
items.why: At alkaline pH, hemoglobins carry a net negative charge and move toward the anode at rates set by their charge. **Of these four, Hb A is the fastest, followed by Hb F, then Hb S, with Hb C slowest and closest to the point of application.** Hb S and Hb C carry fewer negative charges because their beta-chain substitutions remove glutamic acid.

whyNot.0: Hb F migrates slightly behind Hb A at alkaline pH.
whyNot.1: Hb S migrates more slowly than Hb A because valine replaces glutamic acid at beta-6, removing a negative charge.
whyNot.3: Hb C is the slowest of the four because lysine replaces glutamic acid, giving it the least negative charge.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemoglobinopathies chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hemoglobinopathies chapter

items.stem: A woman has microcytosis, a high RBC count, normal ferritin, and suspected beta-thalassemia minor. Which method is preferred to measure her Hb A2 accurately?
options: Alkaline cellulose acetate electrophoresis with visual reading
items.why: Beta-thalassemia minor is diagnosed mainly by an elevated Hb A2, usually above 3.5%. **Cation-exchange HPLC (or microcolumn chromatography) separates and quantifies Hb A2 precisely, which a visual electrophoresis reading cannot do.** Iron deficiency should be ruled out because it can lower Hb A2.

whyNot.0: The solubility test screens for Hb S and gives no quantitative information on Hb A2.
whyNot.1: The Kleihauer-Betke test detects cells containing Hb F, mainly to estimate fetal-maternal hemorrhage.
whyNot.2: On alkaline electrophoresis Hb A2 runs with Hb C and Hb E, and visual estimation of a small band is not precise enough.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., thalassemias chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., thalassemia chapter

items.stem: On a flow cytometry plot of CD45 intensity versus side scatter, where do myeloblasts usually appear?
options: Dim CD45 with low side scatter
Bright CD45 with low side scatter
Moderate CD45 with high side scatter
Negative CD45 with very high side scatter
items.why: CD45 is expressed on all leukocytes, but its intensity increases as cells mature, and side scatter reflects granularity. **Blasts express CD45 weakly and have little granularity, so they fall in a dim-CD45, low-side-scatter region often called the blast gate.** This gating is the first step in most acute leukemia panels.

whyNot.1: Bright CD45 with low side scatter is where mature lymphocytes appear.
whyNot.2: Moderate CD45 with high side scatter is the region of granulocytes, which are heavily granulated.
whyNot.3: CD45-negative events are mainly nucleated red cells or debris, which do not have very high side scatter.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., flow cytometric analysis chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., flow cytometry chapter

items.stem: Blasts from a new acute leukemia are CD34+, HLA-DR+, CD13+, CD33+, and CD117+, and negative for CD19, CD10, and cytoplasmic CD3. Which lineage is indicated?
items.why: CD34 and HLA-DR mark immaturity but are not lineage specific. **CD13, CD33 and CD117 are myeloid-associated antigens, so this pattern indicates myeloid blasts.** The absence of CD19 and cytoplasmic CD3 argues against B- and T-lymphoid lineage.

whyNot.0: B lymphoblasts express CD19, often with CD10, both of which are negative here.
whyNot.2: T lymphoblasts express cytoplasmic CD3, which is negative here.
whyNot.3: Neither B nor T lineage markers are present, so a mixed lymphoid phenotype is not supported.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., flow cytometric analysis chapter; WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours

items.stem: A new technologist is making wedge smears from a patient with a hematocrit of 62%. Her smears are short and thick, with no good thin area. Which change should she make?
options: Use a larger drop and raise the angle of the spreader slide
Use a larger drop and keep the same spreader angle
Use a smaller drop and lower the angle of the spreader slide
Let the drop sit on the slide for a minute before spreading
items.why: Blood with a high hematocrit is viscous and makes thick, short smears. **Lowering the spreader angle (and using a smaller drop, spread smoothly) gives a longer, thinner film with a usable feathered edge.** For a very low hematocrit, the opposite adjustment is made by raising the angle.

whyNot.0: A larger drop and a steeper angle make the film even shorter and thicker; raising the angle is the adjustment for anemic blood, not viscous blood.
whyNot.1: A larger drop puts more viscous blood on the slide and makes the film even thicker.
whyNot.3: Letting the drop sit allows cells to settle and the drop to dry at the edges, causing uneven distribution.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., blood smear preparation chapter; CLSI H20

items.stem: A marrow aspirate from a patient with suspected CML yields no analyzable metaphases after culture. Which test can still detect the BCR-ABL1 fusion directly in non-dividing cells?
items.why: Conventional karyotyping requires cells that divide in culture so chromosomes can be seen in metaphase. **FISH uses fluorescent DNA probes that bind target sequences in interphase nuclei, so it can detect a BCR-ABL1 fusion even when no metaphases are available.** Dual-color fusion probes show the BCR and ABL1 signals joined together.

whyNot.0: Karyotyping needs metaphase cells, which this culture failed to produce.
whyNot.1: Sudan black B stains lipids in granulocytic cells and gives no genetic information.
whyNot.2: Hemoglobin electrophoresis studies globin variants and has no role in detecting translocations.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., cytogenetics and molecular diagnostics chapters; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., cytogenetics chapter

items.stem: After a technologist reviews a smear under oil immersion and switches back to the 40x high-dry objective, the image stays hazy and cannot be focused sharply. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Oil on the 40x lens; clean it with lens paper
Iris diaphragm fully open; close it completely
Light bulb nearing failure; replace the lamp
Condenser set too high; lower it fully
items.why: The 40x objective is a dry lens with a short working distance, and it easily touches oil left on the slide. **Oil on a dry objective blurs the image, so the lens should be cleaned with lens paper (with lens cleaner if needed).** Using only lens paper protects the lens coatings.

whyNot.1: An open diaphragm increases light and may lower contrast, but it does not cause a hazy, unfocusable image; closing it fully would make the field too dark.
whyNot.2: A failing bulb dims the field evenly but does not stop the image from coming into focus.
whyNot.3: Lowering the condenser to its bottom stop reduces resolution and light; a raised condenser is normal for brightfield work.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., microscopy chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., microscopy and laboratory equipment chapter

items.stem: A rural clinic uses a handheld point-of-care hemoglobin photometer with dry-reagent microcuvettes (HemoCue type). What is the measuring principle?
options: Hemoglobin is calculated from a conductivity-based hematocrit
Hemoglobin is converted to azidemethemoglobin and read photometrically
A drop of blood is timed as it falls through copper sulfate
Hemoglobin is converted to acid hematin and matched to a color block
items.why: The microcuvette contains dried reagents that lyse the cells and convert hemoglobin. **Sodium nitrite oxidizes hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which combines with azide to form azidemethemoglobin, read at about 570 nm with a second wavelength to correct for turbidity.** The method correlates well with the cyanmethemoglobin reference method.

whyNot.0: Conductivity-derived hematocrit is used in some blood gas and POC chemistry analyzers, not in these hemoglobin photometers.
whyNot.2: The copper sulfate specific-gravity test is a qualitative donor screen, not a photometric measurement.
whyNot.3: Acid hematin with visual comparison is the old Sahli method, not a photometric point-of-care method.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., hemoglobin determination and point-of-care testing sections; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., hematology procedures chapter

items.stem: On a well-made Wright-stained smear, 72 platelets are seen per 1,000 red cells. The patient's RBC count is 4.0 x 10^12/L. What is the platelet count by this indirect method?
items.why: The indirect method multiplies the platelet-to-red cell ratio on the smear by the RBC count. 72 / 1,000 = 0.072 platelets per red cell. **0.072 x 4.0 x 10^12/L = 2.88 x 10^11/L, which is 288 x 10^9/L.**

whyNot.0: This reports the number of platelets seen without multiplying by the RBC count.
whyNot.1: This is ten times too low; it treats the ratio as 72 per 10,000 red cells.
whyNot.3: This is ten times too high; it treats the ratio as 72 per 100 red cells.

worked.problem: A smear shows 35 platelets per 1,000 RBCs; the RBC count is 3.6 x 10^12/L. Find the platelet count.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., peripheral blood smear examination chapter

items.stem: A patient on chemotherapy has a WBC count of 0.6 x 10^9/L, and a routine wedge smear shows only a few white cells per slide. What is the best way to obtain a smear for a reliable differential?
options: Make thicker wedge smears with a larger drop of blood
Count 25 cells on the routine smear and report percentages
Prepare a thick smear as used for malaria parasites
Prepare smears from the buffy coat of a centrifuged sample
items.why: When the WBC count is very low, a routine smear does not contain enough white cells for a meaningful differential. **Centrifuging the blood and smearing the buffy coat concentrates the leukocytes.** Even so, a reduced count (for example 50 cells) may be reported, with a note.

whyNot.0: Thick wedge smears distort cell morphology and do not concentrate white cells enough to help.
whyNot.1: A 25-cell differential is statistically unreliable; percentages based on so few cells have very wide error.
whyNot.2: Thick smears lyse red cells and distort leukocytes; they are designed to detect parasites, not to perform differentials.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., blood smear preparation chapter; CLSI H20

items.stem: Before starting a differential, a technologist scans a wedge smear under the 10x objective. Which part of the smear should be checked specifically for platelet clumps and large abnormal cells?
options: The feathered edge and the lateral edges
The thick area near the drop origin
The exact center of the smear
The zone where red cells overlap in thick layers
items.why: During wedge spreading, large cells and platelet aggregates are pushed to the edges of the film. **Scanning the feathered edge and the lateral edges at low power detects platelet clumps, blasts, and other large cells that would be missed in the counting area.** The differential itself is done in the thin area where red cells just touch.

whyNot.1: The thick area is too crowded to see cells well, and large cells are carried away from it.
whyNot.2: The center is not where large cells and clumps collect, so this check would miss them.
whyNot.3: Areas with overlapping red cells are too thick for morphology and are not where platelet clumps gather.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., peripheral blood smear examination chapter; CLSI H20

items.stem: A smear shows red cells stacked like coins. To find out whether this is rouleaux or true agglutination, a technologist replaces the plasma with saline and examines a wet preparation. Which result indicates rouleaux?
options: The cells remain in irregular clumps in saline
The stacks disperse into single cells in saline
The cells disperse only after warming to 37 degrees C
The cells lyse completely in saline
items.why: Rouleaux are caused by abnormal plasma proteins, such as the paraprotein of multiple myeloma, that reduce the repulsion between red cells. **Removing the plasma and adding saline breaks up rouleaux, whereas antibody-mediated agglutination persists.** Agglutination that disperses on warming suggests a cold autoantibody.

whyNot.0: Clumps that persist after saline replacement are typical of agglutination by antibody.
whyNot.2: Dispersal only on warming points to cold agglutinins, a form of agglutination, not rouleaux.
whyNot.3: Normal red cells do not lyse in isotonic saline; lysis would point to a different problem.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., peripheral blood smear examination chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., red cell morphology chapter

items.stem: A patient with sudden thrombocytopenia has a smear review for schistocytes. Following ICSH guidance, the technologist counts 1,000 red cells and finds 14 schistocytes. How should this be interpreted?
options: 14%; far above the cutoff, typical of mechanical heart valves
0.14%; within the range seen in healthy adults
1.4%; above the ICSH 1% cutoff, supporting thrombotic microangiopathy
items.why: ICSH recommends counting schistocytes in at least 1,000 red cells and reporting a percentage: 14 / 1,000 x 100 = 1.4%. **In adults, a schistocyte count above 1% strongly suggests thrombotic microangiopathy when the clinical picture fits.** Only typical fragments, such as helmet cells, triangles, and microspherocytes in their presence, should be counted.

whyNot.0: This places the decimal wrongly; 14 of 1,000 cells is 1.4%, not 14%.
whyNot.1: This places the decimal wrongly in the other direction; 14 of 1,000 is 1.4%.
whyNot.3: The ICSH threshold in adults is 1%, not 5%; a count of 1.4% is significant.

items.ref: ICSH recommendations for identification and quantitation of schistocytes (Zini et al., 2012; updated 2021); Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., red cell morphology chapter

items.stem: An impedance analyzer measures RBC 4.40 x 10^12/L, MCV 90 fL, and hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL. Which hematocrit and MCHC will it report?
items.why: Automated analyzers do not spin the blood; they calculate hematocrit from the measured RBC count and MCV. Hct (%) = RBC x MCV / 10 = 4.40 x 90 / 10 = 39.6%. **MCHC = Hb / Hct x 100 = 12.8 / 39.6 x 100 = 32.3 g/dL.**

whyNot.0: This divides MCV by RBC instead of multiplying, which gives an impossible MCHC.
whyNot.1: This uses the rule of three (Hb x 3) to estimate hematocrit; the analyzer uses RBC x MCV.
whyNot.2: The hematocrit is right, but 29.1 is the MCH (Hb / RBC x 10, in pg), not the MCHC.

worked.problem: An analyzer measures RBC 5.10 x 10^12/L, MCV 82 fL, and Hb 13.6 g/dL. Find the reported Hct and MCHC.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., automation in hematology chapter

items.stem: A grossly lipemic specimen gives Hb 15.8 g/dL, Hct 36%, MCH 38 pg, and MCHC 44 g/dL. The smear shows normochromic, normocytic red cells. What should the technologist do?
options: Replace the plasma with an equal volume of diluent and rerun
Warm the specimen to 37 degrees C for 30 minutes and rerun
Dilute the specimen 1:2 with distilled water and multiply by 2
Report the results with a comment about spherocytes
items.why: Lipid droplets cause turbidity in the hemoglobin channel and raise the hemoglobin reading, which then raises MCH and MCHC. **Plasma replacement (spin, remove plasma, add an equal volume of diluent, mix and rerun) removes the lipid and gives a correct hemoglobin.** The red cell count and MCV are not affected by lipemia.

whyNot.1: Warming corrects interference by cold agglutinins, not by lipemia.
whyNot.2: Water would lyse the red cells and does not remove the lipid that causes turbidity.
whyNot.3: The smear shows normal cells, and an MCHC of 44 g/dL is not physiologic, so the results must not be reported as true.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., automation in hematology chapter

items.stem: An impedance analyzer reports a platelet count of 62 x 10^9/L with a flag. The WBC is 11.8 x 10^9/L, and the WBC histogram shows an abnormal rise at its far left edge, below the 35 fL discriminator. The patient's platelet count was normal yesterday. Which interference is most likely?
options: Microcytic red cells counted as platelets
Platelet clumps counted as small white cells
Cold agglutinin doublets counted as one large red cell
items.why: Large platelet aggregates are too big to fall in the platelet channel and may be counted in the white cell channel. **This gives a falsely low platelet count, a falsely high WBC, and a peak at the left edge of the WBC histogram.** The smear should be checked for clumps and the sample recollected (for example in citrate) if they are confirmed.

whyNot.0: Microcytic red cells counted as platelets would raise the platelet count, not lower it.
whyNot.2: Lipemia affects the hemoglobin and its indices, not the platelet count or the WBC histogram.
whyNot.3: Cold agglutinin doublets distort the RBC count and MCV; they do not explain a low platelet count with a left-edge WBC peak.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., automation in hematology chapter

items.stem: Many hematology analyzers use hydrodynamic focusing, in which a stream of sheath fluid surrounds the diluted sample. What is its main purpose?
options: To lyse red cells before the white cells are counted
To stain nucleic acids so reticulocytes can be identified
To pass cells singly through the center of the sensing zone
To warm the sample to body temperature before counting
items.why: Without focusing, two cells may pass the sensor together or pass near the edge, giving distorted pulses. **Sheath fluid narrows the sample stream so cells pass in single file through the center of the aperture or flow cell.** This reduces coincidence errors and recirculation and makes pulse size more consistent.

whyNot.0: Red cells are lysed by a lytic reagent in the WBC channel, not by the sheath fluid.
whyNot.1: Reticulocytes are identified with fluorescent or supravital dyes added to the sample, not by sheath flow.
whyNot.3: Sheath flow does not control the temperature of the sample.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology: Clinical Principles and Applications, 6th ed., automated blood cell analysis chapter; McKenzie's Clinical Laboratory Hematology, 4th ed., automation in hematology chapter

items.stem: Which embryonic hemoglobin is made of two zeta and two epsilon globin chains?
items.why: Embryonic hemoglobins are produced by yolk sac-derived erythroblasts before the switch to fetal hemoglobin. **Hb Gower-1 has the composition zeta2 epsilon2.** As the liver becomes the main site of erythropoiesis, gamma-chain production rises and Hb F becomes the main hemoglobin.

whyNot.0: Hb Portland is zeta2 gamma2; it contains gamma chains rather than epsilon chains.
whyNot.1: Hb Gower-2 is alpha2 epsilon2, so it carries alpha chains rather than zeta chains.
whyNot.2: Hb Barts is a gamma4 tetramer formed when alpha chains are lacking, as in severe alpha-thalassemia; it is not a normal embryonic hemoglobin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hemoglobin metabolism chapter

items.stem: A 500-cell bone marrow differential gives these counts: granulocytic cells at all stages (myeloblasts through segmented neutrophils, plus eosinophils and basophils) 240, nucleated erythroid precursors 200, lymphocytes 40, monocytes 15, and plasma cells 5. The laboratory's adult reference interval for the myeloid-to-erythroid (M:E) ratio is 1.5:1 to 3.3:1. What is the M:E ratio, and how is it interpreted?
items.why: The M:E ratio compares all granulocytic cells and their precursors with nucleated erythroid precursors; lymphocytes, monocytes, and plasma cells are left out. Here 240 / 200 = 1.2, so **the M:E ratio is 1.2:1, below the reference interval**. A low ratio means relatively more erythroid activity (as after hemolysis or blood loss) or reduced granulocyte production.

whyNot.0: This divides erythroid by myeloid cells, inverting the ratio; a value below 1 would in any case mean erythroid excess, not myeloid hyperplasia.
whyNot.1: This adds the lymphocytes to the erythroid side; lymphocytes belong to neither side of the ratio.
whyNot.3: This adds lymphocytes and monocytes to the myeloid side; only granulocytic cells are counted as myeloid.

worked.problem: A 400-cell marrow differential has 270 granulocytic cells (all stages), 90 nucleated erythroid precursors, 30 lymphocytes, 6 monocytes, and 4 plasma cells. Find the M:E ratio.
steps: Leave out lymphocytes, monocytes, and plasma cells

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, bone marrow examination chapter

items.stem: A core biopsy from a 75-year-old man with mild anemia shows hematopoietic cells filling about 25% of the marrow space, with fat in the rest. All cell lines are present and maturing normally. How should the cellularity be reported?
options: Hypocellular, because adult marrow should be about 50% cellular
items.why: Marrow cellularity falls with age as fat replaces hematopoietic tissue; a common rule of thumb puts the expected cellularity at roughly 100 minus the patient's age, in percent. For a 75-year-old, about 25% is expected, so **this marrow is normocellular for age**. Judging it against a young-adult value would wrongly label it hypocellular.

whyNot.1: About 50% cellularity is typical of younger adults; applying it at age 75 ignores the normal age-related increase in marrow fat.
whyNot.2: Hypercellularity would require hematopoietic tissue clearly above the roughly 25% expected at his age.
whyNot.3: Aplastic anemia needs a markedly hypocellular marrow for age with significant cytopenias; normal trilineage maturation at an age-appropriate cellularity does not fit.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, bone marrow examination chapter

items.stem: Before a peripheral blood stem cell collection, the transplant team asks the laboratory to count circulating hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells by flow cytometry. Which marker is counted?
items.why: Hematopoietic stem cells and early progenitors express CD34, a surface glycoprotein that is lost as cells mature. **Flow cytometric CD34 enumeration is the standard measure of stem cell content** in blood and apheresis products. The count guides the timing of collection and whether the graft is adequate.

whyNot.0: CD3 is a pan-T-cell marker found on mature T lymphocytes.
whyNot.1: CD19 is a B-lineage marker.
whyNot.3: CD41 (GPIIb) marks megakaryocytes and platelets.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hematopoiesis and flow cytometry chapters

items.stem: While scanning a posterior iliac crest aspirate from a child, a technologist finds a very large cell with abundant granular cytoplasm and about eight separate, round, similar-sized nuclei that do not touch one another. What is this cell most likely to be?
items.why: Osteoclasts are bone-resorbing giant cells formed by fusion of monocyte-macrophage precursors, so **many separate, round, uniform nuclei identify an osteoclast**. A megakaryocyte, by contrast, has one large nucleus whose lobes remain connected. Osteoclasts and osteoblasts are seen more often in aspirates from children, whose bones are actively remodeling.

whyNot.0: A megakaryocyte becomes polyploid by endomitosis, giving one lobulated nucleus rather than several separate nuclei.
whyNot.2: Osteoblasts have a single eccentric nucleus and resemble plasma cells; they are not multinucleated.
whyNot.3: Gaucher cells are lipid-laden macrophages with one or a few small nuclei and wrinkled, striated cytoplasm.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, bone marrow examination chapter

items.stem: A 25-year-old has had bluish lips since childhood but no shortness of breath. His blood is chocolate-brown, arterial pO2 is normal, and methemoglobin is 18%. His brother has the same findings. Deficiency of which enzyme best explains this?
items.why: The methemoglobin reductase pathway uses NADH and cytochrome b5 reductase to return oxidized (ferric) heme iron to the ferrous state. **Inherited deficiency of NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase causes lifelong methemoglobinemia**, often with cyanosis but few symptoms. A normal pO2 with chocolate-brown blood points to abnormal hemoglobin rather than lung disease.

whyNot.1: G6PD deficiency limits NADPH and causes episodes of oxidant hemolysis with Heinz bodies; it does not cause lifelong methemoglobinemia, although it makes methylene blue treatment ineffective.
whyNot.2: Pyruvate kinase deficiency lowers ATP from glycolysis and causes chronic hemolytic anemia, not cyanosis from methemoglobin.
whyNot.3: Bisphosphoglycerate mutase makes 2,3-BPG; its deficiency raises oxygen affinity and can cause erythrocytosis, not methemoglobinemia.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, erythrocyte metabolism and membrane chapter

items.stem: Within an hour of an ABO-incompatible red cell transfusion, a patient develops fever, back pain, and red-brown urine. Which set of results reflects intravascular hemolysis?
options: Haptoglobin increased, plasma free hemoglobin normal, urine hemoglobin negative
Haptoglobin normal, plasma free hemoglobin normal, urine bilirubin strongly positive
Haptoglobin increased, plasma free hemoglobin increased, urine hemoglobin positive
Haptoglobin decreased, plasma free hemoglobin increased, urine hemoglobin positive
items.why: When red cells lyse inside vessels, free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin and the complex is quickly cleared, so haptoglobin falls. **Once haptoglobin is saturated, free hemoglobin rises in plasma and passes into the urine as hemoglobinuria.** Hemosiderinuria follows several days later as renal tubular cells shed stored iron.

whyNot.0: Haptoglobin can rise as an acute-phase protein, but brisk intravascular hemolysis consumes it; normal plasma hemoglobin and negative urine hemoglobin do not fit red-brown urine.
whyNot.1: Unconjugated bilirubin from hemolysis is bound to albumin and does not enter urine, so urine bilirubin is not a hemolysis marker; haptoglobin and plasma hemoglobin would also be abnormal.
whyNot.2: Haptoglobin binds and removes free hemoglobin, so it falls rather than rises when plasma hemoglobin is high.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hemolytic anemia (intravascular and extravascular hemolysis) chapter

items.stem: A child who has been eating paint chips has microcytic anemia, coarse basophilic stippling, increased zinc protoporphyrin, and increased urine delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA). Lead blocks which two enzymes of heme synthesis to produce this pattern?
items.why: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase, so ALA builds up and spills into the urine, and it inhibits ferrochelatase, so iron cannot be inserted and zinc is placed into protoporphyrin instead. **Inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase explains the high urine ALA and zinc protoporphyrin.** Lead also inhibits pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase, leaving undegraded RNA that shows as coarse basophilic stippling.

whyNot.0: ALA synthase is the first, rate-limiting enzyme; if lead blocked it, ALA would fall rather than accumulate in urine.
whyNot.2: Deficiencies of these enzymes cause acute intermittent porphyria and porphyria cutanea tarda; they are not the main lead targets.
whyNot.3: Blocking ALA synthase would lower ALA rather than raise it; the hallmark lead targets are ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hemoglobin metabolism and disorders of iron and heme chapters

items.stem: A firefighter rescued from a house fire has a headache and confusion. His pulse oximeter reads 98%, but co-oximetry shows 28% carboxyhemoglobin. How does carbon monoxide impair oxygen delivery?
options: It oxidizes heme iron to the ferric state and shifts the curve to the right
It binds heme irreversibly and denatures the globin chains
It binds heme far more tightly than O2 and shifts the dissociation curve to the left
It binds the globin chains and shifts the curve to the right
items.why: Carbon monoxide binds heme iron with roughly 200 to 250 times the affinity of oxygen, so less hemoglobin is available to carry O2. **It also raises the oxygen affinity of the remaining hemes, shifting the curve to the left** so tissues receive even less oxygen. Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, which explains the falsely normal reading.

whyNot.0: Oxidation of heme iron to Fe3+ describes methemoglobin formation by oxidant drugs or nitrites, not carbon monoxide.
whyNot.1: Irreversible change with denatured globin describes sulfhemoglobin; carbon monoxide binding is reversible and clears with oxygen therapy.
whyNot.3: Binding to globin amino groups is how carbon dioxide is carried; carbon monoxide binds the heme iron and shifts the curve to the left.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hemoglobin metabolism chapter

items.stem: During a family study for thalassemia, which statement about the location of the human globin genes is correct?
options: Alpha and zeta genes are on chromosome 11; beta, gamma, delta, and epsilon genes are on chromosome 16
Alpha and zeta genes are on chromosome 16; beta, gamma, delta, and epsilon genes are on chromosome 11
Alpha and gamma genes are on chromosome 16; beta, delta, epsilon, and zeta genes are on chromosome 11
All of the globin genes lie in a single cluster on chromosome 11
items.why: **The alpha-like genes (zeta and two alpha genes) lie on chromosome 16, and the beta-like genes (epsilon, two gamma, delta, and beta) lie on chromosome 11.** Each person therefore has four alpha genes, which is why alpha-thalassemia severity depends on how many are deleted. Beta-thalassemia involves the single beta gene on each chromosome 11.

whyNot.0: This reverses the two gene clusters.
whyNot.2: Gamma genes belong to the beta-like cluster on chromosome 11, and zeta belongs to the alpha-like cluster on chromosome 16.
whyNot.3: The alpha-like and beta-like genes are on different chromosomes, so chain production must be balanced between two loci.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, hemoglobin metabolism chapter

items.stem: A marrow aspirate from a patient with a chronic infection shows increased plasma cells. Each has an eccentric nucleus with coarse chromatin, deep blue cytoplasm, and a pale zone beside the nucleus. What does this pale perinuclear zone represent?
items.why: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B cells devoted to antibody production. Abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum makes the cytoplasm deeply basophilic, while **the pale perinuclear hof is the prominent Golgi apparatus** where immunoglobulin is processed for secretion. The hof is a key feature for recognizing plasma cells on a smear.

whyNot.0: Russell bodies are round globules of condensed immunoglobulin scattered in the cytoplasm, not a pale zone beside the nucleus.
whyNot.1: Lysosomes are not prominent in plasma cells and do not form a clear area next to the nucleus.
whyNot.2: Glycogen is shown with the PAS stain and does not form the perinuclear clear zone.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, leukocyte development (lymphocytes and plasma cells) chapter

items.stem: Circulating monocytes leave the blood and mature into tissue macrophages whose names depend on where they live. What are the resident macrophages that line the liver sinusoids called?
items.why: Monocytes circulate only briefly before entering tissues, where they become macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system. **In the liver, the macrophages lining the sinusoids are Kupffer cells**, which remove aged cells, debris, and bacteria from portal blood.

whyNot.1: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system.
whyNot.2: Osteoclasts are multinucleated bone-resorbing cells of the monocyte-macrophage lineage found in bone.
whyNot.3: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting dendritic cells of the epidermis.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, leukocyte development (monocytes and macrophages) chapter

items.stem: A 19-year-old with fever, sore throat, and enlarged lymph nodes has many large lymphocytes with abundant blue cytoplasm that scallops around neighboring red cells. The heterophile antibody test is positive. Which cells make up most of these reactive lymphocytes?
options: B cells directly infected by EBV
Natural killer cells activated by interferon
Cytotoxic T cells reacting to EBV-infected B cells
items.why: Epstein-Barr virus enters B cells through the CD21 receptor. **The reactive lymphocytes seen in the blood are mostly CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells** proliferating in response to the infected B cells. Their varied, polyclonal, transient nature separates them from a lymphoid neoplasm.

whyNot.0: EBV infects B cells, but infected B cells are relatively few in the blood; the large scalloped cells are mainly reactive T cells.
whyNot.1: NK cells take part in the response, but they are a minor fraction of the reactive lymphocytes.
whyNot.3: A heterophile-positive picture with varied reactive forms is a benign polyclonal response, not a lymphoblastic leukemia.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, nonmalignant leukocyte disorders chapter

items.stem: Which peripheral blood leukocyte carries high-affinity IgE receptors and has dark purple-black granules containing histamine and heparin that may dissolve during water-based staining?
items.why: Basophils have large metachromatic granules rich in histamine and heparin and bind IgE through high-affinity Fc-epsilon receptors. **These features make the basophil a circulating effector of immediate (type I) hypersensitivity.** Because the granules are water-soluble, they can wash out during staining and leave empty-looking areas in the cytoplasm.

whyNot.0: Eosinophils have orange-red granules containing major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein, not mainly histamine and heparin.
whyNot.1: Neutrophil granules contain myeloperoxidase, lysozyme, and lactoferrin and stain lilac to pink.
whyNot.2: Monocytes have fine azurophilic granules in gray-blue cytoplasm, without large histamine-containing granules.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, leukocyte development chapter

items.stem: Within hours of a bacterial infection, a patient's neutrophil count rises and band forms increase, well before new myeloblasts could have matured. Which marrow compartment supplies these cells?
options: The storage pool of metamyelocytes, bands, and segmented neutrophils
The mitotic pool of myeloblasts, promyelocytes, and myelocytes
The stem cell pool of CD34-positive progenitors
The tissue pool of neutrophils already in the tissues
items.why: Granulopoiesis has a mitotic (proliferating) pool, from myeloblast to myelocyte, and a post-mitotic maturation and storage pool. **The marrow storage pool holds several days' supply of non-dividing neutrophils and bands that can be released quickly**, which explains the rapid neutrophilia with a left shift in infection. Increased production from the mitotic pool takes days to add cells.

whyNot.1: Cells in the mitotic pool still need several days of division and maturation before release, so they cannot explain a rise within hours.
whyNot.2: Stem and progenitor cells must pass through all maturation stages first and are not released as functional neutrophils.
whyNot.3: Neutrophils that have migrated into tissues do not return to the blood.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, leukocyte development (neutrophil kinetics) chapter

items.stem: Megakaryocytes become very large cells with up to 32N or 64N DNA content. By what process does this polyploidy develop?
options: Repeated mitosis with complete cell division
Nuclear budding into separate daughter cells
items.why: Megakaryocytes replicate their DNA repeatedly but do not complete nuclear separation or cytoplasmic division. **This endomitosis produces one large, lobulated, polyploid nucleus.** Higher ploidy goes with larger cell size and greater platelet output.

whyNot.0: Cell fusion produces multinucleated cells such as osteoclasts, which have many separate nuclei rather than one lobulated nucleus.
whyNot.1: Mitosis with cell division would produce more cells of normal ploidy, not one giant polyploid cell.
whyNot.3: Budding describes platelet release from proplatelet extensions of the cytoplasm, not the development of nuclear polyploidy.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, megakaryopoiesis and platelet production chapter

items.stem: When platelets are activated, they release an alpha-granule protein that binds heparin with high affinity and neutralizes its anticoagulant effect. Which protein is this?
items.why: Platelet factor 4 (PF4) is a positively charged chemokine stored in alpha granules. **PF4 binds heparin tightly and neutralizes it**, and complexes of PF4 with heparin are the antigen recognized in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Plasma PF4, like beta-thromboglobulin, can be measured as a marker of platelet activation.

whyNot.0: Beta-thromboglobulin is another platelet-specific alpha-granule protein used as an activation marker, but it is not the main heparin-neutralizing protein.
whyNot.2: ADP is stored in dense granules and promotes aggregation; it has no heparin-neutralizing action.
whyNot.3: Thrombospondin is an alpha-granule adhesive glycoprotein whose main role is stabilizing aggregates, not neutralizing heparin.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, platelet structure and function chapter

items.stem: Within the platelet, which membrane system sequesters calcium ions and contains the cyclooxygenase and thromboxane synthase that convert arachidonic acid to thromboxane A2?
items.why: The dense tubular system is derived from the megakaryocyte's endoplasmic reticulum and stays within the platelet. **It stores calcium and is the site of prostaglandin and thromboxane A2 synthesis**, so it controls key activation signals. The open canalicular system, in contrast, is a network of channels connected to the surface.

whyNot.1: The open canalicular system connects to the surface; it adds membrane area and is a route for granule release, not the calcium store.
whyNot.2: The glycocalyx is the outer surface coat carrying glycoprotein receptors and adsorbed plasma proteins.
whyNot.3: The circumferential microtubule band maintains the resting disc shape and is not a membrane system.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, platelet structure and function chapter

items.stem: Resting platelets keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. After strong activation, it moves to the outer surface. What is the main hemostatic effect of this change?
options: It provides binding sites for von Willebrand factor during adhesion
It blocks fibrinogen binding to GPIIb/IIIa to limit aggregation
It is the direct substrate of cyclooxygenase for thromboxane synthesis
It provides a negative surface for assembling tenase and prothrombinase
items.why: Exposed phosphatidylserine gives the activated platelet a negatively charged surface. **Vitamin K-dependent factors bind this surface through calcium bridges, assembling the tenase (IXa-VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa-Va) complexes** that generate thrombin. This procoagulant activity was historically called platelet factor 3.

whyNot.0: VWF binds the GPIb-IX-V complex, not phosphatidylserine.
whyNot.1: Activation increases, rather than blocks, fibrinogen binding to GPIIb/IIIa.
whyNot.2: Cyclooxygenase acts on arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2; phosphatidylserine exposure is a separate event.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, platelet structure and function chapter

items.stem: Blood allowed to clot in a glass tube normally shrinks over the next hour and expels serum. Which mechanism drives this clot retraction?
options: Factor XIIIa cross-linking adjacent fibrin strands
Platelet actomyosin pulling on GPIIb/IIIa-bound fibrin
Plasmin digesting fibrin at the edges of the clot
items.why: Activated platelets attach to fibrin through GPIIb/IIIa and contract their actin-myosin (thrombosthenin) filaments. **This platelet contraction pulls the fibrin strands together and squeezes out serum.** Clot retraction is therefore poor in severe thrombocytopenia and in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

whyNot.0: Factor XIIIa stabilizes fibrin with covalent cross-links but does not contract the clot.
whyNot.2: Plasmin dissolves the clot (fibrinolysis) rather than retracting it.
whyNot.3: Fibrinopeptide release lets fibrin monomers polymerize; it forms the clot but does not shrink it.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, platelet structure and function chapter

items.stem: A woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL and MCV 82 fL. Which set of iron results best fits anemia of chronic inflammation?
options: Serum iron decreased, TIBC increased, ferritin decreased
Serum iron increased, TIBC decreased, ferritin increased
Serum iron decreased, TIBC decreased, ferritin normal or increased
Serum iron normal, TIBC normal or increased, ferritin decreased
items.why: In chronic inflammation, interleukin-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks iron release from macrophages and iron absorption from the gut. **Serum iron is low while storage iron (ferritin) is normal or high, and TIBC is low or normal.** Iron deficiency differs because TIBC rises and ferritin falls.

whyNot.0: This is the iron deficiency pattern, with depleted stores and a compensatory rise in transferrin.
whyNot.1: High serum iron with high ferritin fits iron overload, as in hemochromatosis or sideroblastic anemia.
whyNot.3: A low ferritin indicates depleted stores, as in early iron deficiency, rather than iron held in macrophages.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, disorders of iron kinetics and heme metabolism chapter

items.stem: A 24-year-old woman with no symptoms has hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, RBC 6.10 x 10^12/L, MCV 63 fL, MCH 18.7 pg, and RDW 13.4% (reference 11.5-14.5%). Serum ferritin is 80 ng/mL. Which condition is most likely?
items.why: Marked microcytosis with a high RBC count and a normal RDW is typical of thalassemia trait. The Mentzer index (MCV / RBC) is 63 / 6.10 = 10.3, and **a value below 13 favors thalassemia trait over iron deficiency**; the normal ferritin also argues against iron deficiency. Hb A2 quantitation (raised in beta-thalassemia trait) or DNA testing for alpha-thalassemia identifies the type.

whyNot.0: Iron deficiency usually gives a low RBC count, a raised RDW, a Mentzer index above 13, and a low ferritin.
whyNot.2: Anemia of chronic inflammation is normocytic or mildly microcytic with a low RBC count, not an MCV of 63 fL with a high RBC count.
whyNot.3: Sideroblastic anemia typically shows a dimorphic red cell population with a raised RDW, high iron and ferritin, and ringed sideroblasts in the marrow.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, thalassemias chapter

items.stem: Several weeks after treatment with chloramphenicol, a patient has hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL, WBC 1.6 x 10^9/L, platelets 18 x 10^9/L, and a corrected reticulocyte count of 0.2%. There is no splenomegaly and no abnormal cells on the smear. A marrow biopsy is about 10% cellular and mostly fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Aplastic anemia is failure of hematopoietic stem cells, giving pancytopenia with a very low reticulocyte count. **A hypocellular, fat-filled marrow without abnormal cells confirms marrow failure** rather than peripheral destruction or marrow infiltration. Drugs such as chloramphenicol, benzene exposure, and radiation are classic acquired causes.

whyNot.0: Megaloblastic anemia can cause pancytopenia, but the marrow is hypercellular with megaloblasts, and the blood shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
whyNot.1: Hypersplenism causes cytopenias by splenic pooling, so splenomegaly and a normal or hypercellular marrow would be expected.
whyNot.2: Primary myelofibrosis usually shows splenomegaly, teardrop cells, a leukoerythroblastic smear, and a fibrotic marrow, often with a dry tap.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, bone marrow failure chapter

items.stem: An adult with fatigue and cytopenias has 12% myeloblasts in the bone marrow, some with Auer rods. Cytogenetics shows t(8;21)(q22;q22.1), producing a RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion. Under the WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours (5th edition, 2022), how is this classified?
items.why: WHO 5e divides AML into types defined by genetic abnormalities and types defined by differentiation. **For most defining genetic abnormalities, including RUNX1::RUNX1T1, AML is diagnosed whatever the blast percentage**; the 20% cutoff still applies to AML defined by differentiation and to a few genetic types such as BCR::ABL1 fusion and CEBPA mutation. A 12% blast count therefore does not place this case in MDS.

whyNot.1: MDS-IB2 covers 10-19% marrow blasts, but it cannot be diagnosed when an AML-defining fusion such as RUNX1::RUNX1T1 is present.
whyNot.2: MDS-IB1 covers 5-9% marrow blasts, which is below this count, and the defining fusion would override it in any case.
whyNot.3: AML with maturation is a differentiation-defined type, used only when no defining genetic abnormality is found and requiring at least 20% blasts.

items.ref: WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours 5e (2022), myeloid neoplasms (AML with defining genetic abnormalities)

items.stem: A 68-year-old has back pain, hypercalcemia, rising creatinine, and lytic skull lesions. The smear shows marked rouleaux, serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG kappa M-protein, and clonal plasma cells make up 35% of the marrow cells. What is the diagnosis?
items.why: Myeloma is a clonal plasma cell neoplasm that secretes a monoclonal immunoglobulin, which coats red cells and causes rouleaux and a high ESR. **At least 10% clonal marrow plasma cells plus myeloma-related end-organ damage (hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, or bone lesions) defines plasma cell myeloma.** IgG is the most common type of M-protein.

whyNot.0: Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia involves an IgM protein and hyperviscosity; lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia are uncommon.
whyNot.1: MGUS has fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-related end-organ damage.
whyNot.3: CLL is a neoplasm of small mature B lymphocytes with smudge cells; it does not cause lytic lesions with marrow plasmacytosis.

items.ref: WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours 5e (2022), plasma cell neoplasms; Rodak's Hematology 6e, mature lymphoid neoplasms chapter

items.stem: A child with partial albinism and repeated pyogenic infections has neutrophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes containing giant, irregular gray-to-red cytoplasmic granules. Which inherited disorder is most likely?
items.why: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive defect in lysosomal trafficking (LYST gene) in which granules fuse into giant inclusions. **Giant leukocyte granules with partial albinism and frequent infections form the classic picture**; platelets also lack dense granules, so bleeding can occur. The abnormal granules impair killing of ingested bacteria.

whyNot.0: Alder-Reilly granules are dark purple-black mucopolysaccharide deposits seen in mucopolysaccharidoses; they are not linked to albinism, and leukocyte function is normal.
whyNot.1: May-Hegglin anomaly shows pale blue Dohle-like inclusions with giant platelets and thrombocytopenia, not albinism or giant granules.
whyNot.2: Chronic granulomatous disease impairs the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst, but neutrophil morphology is normal.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, nonmalignant leukocyte disorders chapter

items.stem: A young man with lifelong nosebleeds has a platelet count of 70 x 10^9/L, and many platelets on the smear are as large as red cells. Aggregation is normal with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine but absent with ristocetin, and adding normal plasma does not restore the ristocetin response. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is an inherited deficiency of the GPIb-IX-V complex, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor. **Absent ristocetin aggregation that normal plasma does not correct, with giant platelets and mild thrombocytopenia, points to this receptor defect.** Responses to other agonists stay normal because their receptors are intact.

whyNot.1: In von Willebrand disease the defect is in plasma VWF, so normal plasma restores ristocetin aggregation, and platelet size is normal.
whyNot.2: Glanzmann thrombasthenia gives absent aggregation with ADP, collagen, and epinephrine but a normal ristocetin response, with normal platelet count and size.
whyNot.3: Gray platelet syndrome has large pale platelets lacking alpha granules, but ristocetin aggregation is normal.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, qualitative platelet disorders chapter

items.stem: Two weeks after a viral illness, a 5-year-old develops sudden petechiae and bruising. The platelet count is 12 x 10^9/L with some large platelets; hemoglobin, WBC, and the rest of the smear are normal, and the PT and APTT are normal. What is the mechanism of the most likely disorder?
options: Platelets are consumed in widespread microthrombi with clotting factor depletion
Autoantibodies coat platelets, which are cleared by splenic macrophages
Antibodies to PF4-heparin complexes activate platelets
items.why: Childhood immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) often follows a viral infection and begins abruptly with bleeding into the skin. **IgG autoantibodies, often against GPIIb/IIIa, coat platelets that are then removed by splenic macrophages.** The marrow has normal or increased megakaryocytes, young larger platelets appear in the blood, and most children recover within weeks to months.

whyNot.0: Marrow failure would usually affect other cell lines and would not produce large young platelets.
whyNot.1: Consumption with factor depletion describes DIC, which would prolong the PT and APTT.
whyNot.3: Anti-PF4-heparin antibodies cause heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, which needs heparin exposure and causes thrombosis rather than petechiae.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, quantitative platelet disorders chapter

items.stem: An adult has platelet counts near 1,050 x 10^9/L on repeated testing, with normal hemoglobin, WBC, iron studies, and C-reactive protein, and no history of splenectomy. BCR::ABL1 is not detected, a CALR mutation is found, and the marrow shows increased large megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei and no fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.why: Essential thrombocythemia (ET) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with a sustained platelet count of at least 450 x 10^9/L. **A JAK2, CALR, or MPL driver mutation with large hyperlobulated megakaryocytes, after other causes are excluded, supports ET under WHO criteria.** Patients are at risk of both thrombosis and bleeding because platelet function is abnormal.

whyNot.0: Reactive thrombocytosis follows iron deficiency, inflammation, infection, or splenectomy, which were excluded, and it has no clonal driver mutation.
whyNot.2: CML requires the BCR::ABL1 fusion, which is absent here.
whyNot.3: Polycythemia vera requires raised hemoglobin or red cell mass, usually with a JAK2 mutation; hemoglobin is normal here.

items.ref: WHO Classification of Haematolymphoid Tumours 5e (2022), myeloproliferative neoplasms

items.stem: A citrated plasma specimen for factor assays was left uncapped at room temperature for most of the day. Activity of which two factors is most likely to have fallen because they are labile?
items.why: Factors V and VIII are the labile factors and lose activity quickly in plasma kept at room temperature. **Their decay falsely prolongs the PT (factor V) and APTT (factor VIII) and lowers their measured activities.** Coagulation specimens should therefore be tested promptly or the plasma frozen.

whyNot.1: Factors VII and IX are stable in stored plasma; aged plasma still contains them.
whyNot.2: Prothrombin and factor X are stable vitamin K-dependent factors.
whyNot.3: Factors XI and XII are stable in stored plasma and are even present in serum.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, normal hemostasis and coagulation chapter; CLSI H21

items.stem: A clotted red-top tube is centrifuged and the serum is saved as a reagent. Which group of factors is essentially absent from this serum because they are used up during clotting?
options: Factors II, VII, IX, and X
Factors XI, XII, prekallikrein, and HMWK
Factors VII, IX, X, and XII
Factors I, V, VIII, and XIII
items.why: Thrombin acts on fibrinogen and on factors V, VIII, and XIII during clotting, so these fibrinogen-group factors are consumed. **Serum therefore lacks factors I, V, VIII, and XIII**, and most of the prothrombin is also used up. Factors VII, IX, X, XI, and XII remain in serum, which is why aged serum is used in correction studies.

whyNot.0: Factors VII, IX, and X survive clotting and stay in serum; only prothrombin in this group is largely consumed.
whyNot.1: The contact factors are not consumed during clotting and remain in serum.
whyNot.2: These factors all remain in serum, which is why aged serum supplies them in substitution studies.

items.ref: Harmening's Clinical Hematology and Fundamentals of Hemostasis 5e, coagulation factors chapter

items.stem: Normal plasma treated with barium sulfate loses factors II, VII, IX, and X but keeps factors I, V, VIII, XI, XII, and XIII. Why are only the first four removed?
options: They are consumed when the plasma is exposed to barium
Their gamma-carboxyglutamic acid residues bind the barium salt
They circulate bound to von Willebrand factor, which is adsorbed
They are activated by contact with the barium surface
items.why: Factors II, VII, IX, and X undergo vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, which gives them gamma-carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) residues. **These Gla domains bind divalent cations, so the factors attach to barium sulfate or aluminum hydroxide and are removed.** Adsorbed plasma is therefore a source of factors I, V, VIII, XI, XII, and XIII in substitution studies.

whyNot.0: Adsorption does not start clotting; the factors are bound and removed, not consumed.
whyNot.2: VWF carries factor VIII, which stays in adsorbed plasma; the vitamin K-dependent factors are not VWF-bound.
whyNot.3: Barium sulfate does not activate these factors; contact activation involves factor XII, which stays in adsorbed plasma.

items.ref: Harmening's Clinical Hematology and Fundamentals of Hemostasis 5e, coagulation factors chapter

items.stem: In the cell-based model of coagulation, a small amount of thrombin is first made on tissue factor-bearing cells. Where does the large burst of thrombin generation (propagation) then take place?
options: On the tissue factor-bearing cell itself
On the surface of activated platelets
Free in the plasma, away from cell surfaces
items.why: The cell-based model has three overlapping phases: initiation on tissue factor-bearing cells, amplification as the first thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII, and XI, and propagation. **During propagation, tenase and prothrombinase complexes assemble on the activated platelet surface and produce a burst of thrombin.** The model shows platelets and clotting factors working together rather than as separate pathways.

whyNot.0: Intact endothelium with thrombomodulin turns thrombin into an activator of protein C, which limits clotting rather than propagating it.
whyNot.1: The tissue factor-bearing cell supports initiation and makes only a small amount of thrombin before tissue factor pathway inhibitor limits it.
whyNot.3: Coagulation enzymes work efficiently only when assembled on phospholipid surfaces; free in plasma they act slowly and are quickly inhibited.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, normal hemostasis and coagulation chapter

items.stem: A child with type 3 (severe) von Willebrand disease has almost no VWF and a factor VIII activity of only 4%, even though the factor VIII gene is normal. What explains the low factor VIII?
options: VWF is the enzyme that activates factor VIII
Without VWF as a carrier, factor VIII is rapidly cleared from plasma
All type 3 patients form inhibitors against factor VIII
The VWF and factor VIII genes are inherited together on the X chromosome
items.why: In plasma, factor VIII circulates bound to VWF, which protects it from proteolysis and early clearance. **When VWF is absent, the half-life of factor VIII falls sharply, so its activity drops** even though it is produced normally. This is why severe VWD can cause hemophilia-like joint and muscle bleeding and a prolonged APTT.

whyNot.0: Factor VIII is activated by thrombin (and factor Xa), not by VWF.
whyNot.2: Inhibitors are uncommon in VWD and, when they occur, are usually against VWF; they do not explain the low factor VIII at diagnosis.
whyNot.3: The VWF gene is on chromosome 12 and VWD is mostly autosomal; only the factor VIII gene is on the X chromosome.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, von Willebrand disease and hemophilia chapter

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman with no earlier bleeding history develops large bruises. The PT is normal and the APTT is 78 s (reference 25-35 s). A 1:1 mix with normal plasma gives an APTT of 33 s when tested immediately, but 64 s after the mix is incubated for 2 hours at 37 degrees C (incubated normal plasma control: 34 s). What is the most likely cause?
items.why: Correction on the immediate mix followed by prolongation after incubation shows a time- and temperature-dependent inhibitor. **This pattern is typical of an autoantibody against factor VIII (acquired hemophilia A)**, which inactivates factor VIII slowly and is seen in older adults, after childbirth, and with autoimmune disease. A factor VIII assay and a Bethesda titer are the next steps.

whyNot.0: A lupus anticoagulant usually acts immediately, so the immediate mix stays prolonged, and it is associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding.
whyNot.1: A single factor deficiency corrects on mixing and stays corrected after incubation.
whyNot.2: Heparin acts immediately, so the immediate mix would not correct, and the thrombin time would also be prolonged.

items.ref: Rodak's Hematology 6e, laboratory evaluation of hemostasis chapter; CLSI H47

items.stem: In a Bethesda assay, a patient's plasma is diluted 1:16 and incubated with an equal volume of normal pooled plasma for 2 hours at 37 degrees C. The residual factor VIII activity of this mixture is 50% of the control. What is the inhibitor titer?
items.why: One Bethesda unit is the amount of inhibitor that destroys half of the factor VIII in an equal volume of normal plasma during the 2-hour incubation, leaving 50% residual activity. **At a 1:16 dilution with 50% residual activity, the undiluted plasma contains 1 x 16 = 16 BU/mL.** Inhibitors of 5 BU/mL or more are classed as high-titer.

whyNot.0: 1 BU/mL is the titer of the diluted sample; it must be multiplied by the dilution factor of 16.
whyNot.1: This halves the result as if the equal-volume mixing step were an extra dilution; the Bethesda unit definition already includes that step.
whyNot.3: This doubles the result for the mixing step, which the Bethesda unit definition already accounts for.

worked.problem: Patient plasma diluted 1:10 leaves 50% residual factor VIII activity after 2 hours of incubation with an equal volume of normal plasma. Find the inhibitor titer.
steps: By definition, 1 BU/mL leaves 50% residual factor VIII activity
So the diluted plasma contains 1 BU/mL
Multiply by the dilution factor: 1 x 10
